A short time ago I asked a question of the government with reference to the militia going to the tercentenary celebration at Quebec this summer, and I notice a statement in the papers to-day that they are not going. I desire to ask the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) what are the facts. If they are not going, why are they not going? Is it due to the inability of the department to handle the troops, or what is the pause of their not going ?

It is not correct to say that the troops are not going to the tercentenary. It is a fact, however, that the annual camps of instruction will be held as usual throughout the Dominion this year, instead of being held at one common point at or near the city of Quebec, as was proposed. The annual drill of the city regiments will also take place as usual this year. The reason of the change in the programme, which programme I announced briefly to the House three or four weeks ago, is chiefly due to the difficulty of transportation. It will be understood, I am sure, that one of the principal things had in mind in connection with this tercentenary celebration is to bring together the largest number possible of people to Quebec to witness the ceremonies. Some time ago the chairman of the commission called my attention to the fact that the transportation lines, the railways and steamboats, must be left free as far as possible to bring the people to Quebec and take them home again, and he thought it proper to ask the Militia Department to agree not to move any troops on a certain number of days before the celebration began and a certain number of days afterwards. It will be readily understood that such an arrangement would hamper the railway transportation lines very much. An earnest effort was made to see whether the difficulty could be overcome, but it was found it could only be partially overcome. It was therefore thought better that the camps should be held at the usual places of holding camps. As to the statement that has been made that the headquarters of the militia were unable to cope with the mobilization of 25,000 or 30,000 troops at a central point like Quebec, the story is absolutely without foundation, and is entirely absurd. The Militia Department is quite able to mobilize 40,000 troops at a

central point like Quebec, within a few days, if not within a few hours, if the necessity arose. But at a time when tens and hundreds of thousands of people from all over the northern part of this continent will be looking towards Quebec, and have got to be taken there over the railways and steamboat lines, every one will agree that a serious problem is presented ; and owing to the fact that the companies cannot give the necessary accommodation such as we think the militia should have, this part of the programme has been given up. As to what will be done to bring troops to Quebec to take part in the celebration, I am not prepared at this moment to make any announcement. But the Militia Department will be prepared to co-operate with the commission in every way in its power.
That is finally final, is it?
Yes.
Might I be permitted to ask the Minister of Militia if it is the intention of the department to allow the rural corps to go into camp as usual ?
Yes, I intended to say that.

House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Aylesworth for the second reading of Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act and the proposed amendment of Mr. W. J. Roche thereto.

Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid La'urier) rose in this House yesterday to make his speech upon this particular piece of legislation, known as Bill (No. 115), but better known as the Ayles-worth Bill, I was in hopes that he would have had the courage of his convictions and that he would state to this House and the country that he was prepared to withdraw the contentious part of the Bill and allow the business of the House to go on. The right hon. gentleman spoke at some length. I listened to each sentence of his speech but he was prepared to withdraw not even one contentious word, not even one contentious clause of this Bill. I listened to him expecting him to refer to clause No. 1 which deals with the province of Manitoba, the unorganized districts of Ontario and Quebec and the province of British Columbia, but not one word did he utter as regards withdrawing this particular clause. I listened that I might hear him say that he was prepared to withdraw clause No. 17 which refers to the secret ballot, but he failed to mention clause No. 17. Now, Sir, the right hon. gentleman thought he had scored heavily upon the opposition when he said: I am prepared to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Marquette, and when he said that he was prepared, in so far as overlapping portions of the various constituencies in Manitoba were concerned, to refer the question to the judges of the province. I say that the right hon. gentleman did not concede anything there. He gave us nothing but what we enjoy at the present time in the province of Manitoba, fixed by law and on the statute-books of that province. Therefore, the right hon. gentleman has not conceded anything. He has not been so fair as he would try to lead hon. members of this House and the people of this country to believe and I cannot understand for a moment how it has gone broadcast throughout our country in the press that the right hon. gentleman has conceded all the wishes of Manitoba. He has not conceded a single thing. Why. I ask, why has the right hon. gentleman singled out the little province of Manitoba? Why is he so anxious to get a slap at the province of Manitoba? Why is he so anxious to insult the intelligence of the people of Manitoba? The right hon. gentleman has refused to allow the province of Manitoba one stick of timber, one acre of land, one ounce of mineral, one fish that floats in the waters of that province and now he Mr. FIELDING
comes forward and puts his grasping hands upon the franchise of the people and tries to take it from them. I say that we will not tolerate that for one moment. Where did the right hon. gentleman get his information? By whom has he been prompted? He has been prompted by the Liberal contingent from the province of Manitoba led by the ex-premier of that province. He consults them. He accepts everything they say, and there is not one word of truth in their statements. I am surprised that the right hon. gentleman should not have listened to the arguments that have been made on this side of the House, arguments which are backed up by facts and backed up by law; but he accepts the statements, and they are only statements, of hon. gentlemen in the Liberal contingent from the province of Manitoba.
Now, Sir, I intend, for a few moments to refer to these hon. gentlemen. I shall endeavour to take up their arguments one by one. I do not for a moment say I am going to attempt to answer them because they have been answered. They were answered in nearly every case before they were made and it is only a waste of time to undertake to answer these hon. gentlemen. But, first, I shall refer to the hon. gentleman who spoke in this House last night. I refer to the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows). Who is this member for Dauphin ? He is a gentleman who sits over there and he has a monopoly of the timber of the western country. He sits in his seat, not by the will of the people, but through the manipulation of his brother-in-law, the ex-Minister of the Interior, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) who has, by his ingenuity, succeeded in setting back his election and allowing that hon. member for Dauphin to take his seat by acclamation.
Now, Sir, I say to the hon. gentleman : come out, fight fair, come out from behind the large spruce trees, come out I say and let the people of this country tell you whether you shall represent them any longer in this House. And if the hon. member does come out in the open I will venture to say he will not come back to this House if he has to fight as others have to fight in the coming election. The hon. gentleman was very careful to read from his Bible, the AVinnipeg ' Free Press,' and that was about the whole of his speech ; that-was all he had to say. He was very careful to read affidavits one after another and they were affidavits which did not do any credit to the hon. gentleman or his party behind him. Amongst others he read a letter which was written by Mr. Hastings, of Manitoba, and that letter is a fair letter, it is a loyal letter, it is a patriotic letter. But, the outside leader of the Liberal party in the province of Manitoba, Mr. Brown, wrote a letter which he had inserted in the different papers throughout the province arid when I

read that letter I want to ask the members of this House if those who voted for Mr. Brown in the last provincial election did their duty when they voted for any such man. He was writ ins with regard to the flag policy of Premier Roblin and he wrote this letter to the newspapers of Manitoba :
In regard to the flag can you not get interviews with school trustees in your district as to what they think of the teachers being compelled to hoist the flag and take it down with the thermometer at 25 and 40 below?
Is there anything patriotic or loyal about that? Then he wrote to the newspaper editors :
Comment yourself editorially on the subject . and if you do you can send a special marked copy to the 'Free Press' at once so that we may copy your views.
Now in connection with this I will take the liberty to recite two or three verses which were written by a late member of the press gallery-methinks I see him here today-and there is nothing I can say to you that will represent the feeling and sentiment of the people of Manitoba better than the verses I am going to recite. That gentleman wrote the following beautiful words:
Give me the Grand Old Union Jack Baptized in blood and tears;
The flag that o'er a nation free Has waved a thousand years.
More modern flags; with stars and bars As beautiful may be;
But the flag that's waved a thousand years Is good enough for me.
Now, these are the words I want specially to commend to the Prime Minister.
Then may it wave o'er land and sea Through time's eternal space;
Equality and liberty There find abiding place.
That verse represents the sentiment of the people of Manitoba : Equality and liberty. That is all we ask, that is what we are fighting for, that is what we expect to get. But I have a doubt as to whether we shall bfe able to get it from the right hon. gentleman when we take into consideration his past record and dealings with the province of Manitoba. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the day is not far distant, the day will soon come, it will come at the next elections when the people have a chance to express their wishes at the polls and they will make the Prime Minister of Canada dance. He will dance as he never danced before, and the people of the country will waltz him from that side of the House and put him in the opposition benches where he always belonged. So much for the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows).
Take another one of them.

The next hon. gentleman I wish to call your attention to is the hon.
member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway). He sat for twelve long years as Prime Minister of the province of Manitoba.
Where is he to-day ?

I do not know just where he is to-day. A few days ago the hon. gentleman (Air. Greenway) made a speech in this House and he made sweeping statements like all the rest of his speeches. He defied any one to take the lists of the province of Manitoba and compile a federal list out of them. Well, it is the simplest thing in the world to do that. The only trouble that arose was about the overlapping of the voters in the polling subdivisions and all that is necessary to do is to leave the assignment of the voters In their propier divisions to the judges of the land. Yesterday the Prime Minister told us he was willing to do that and we thank him heartily for it, and I say that any man who makes the bold statement that it is impossible to compile the federal lists from the provincial lists is stating what is not true. The hon. gentleman (Air. Greenway) went on to say that the addresses of the different voters in Alanitoba are not given on the lists. I am prepared to admit that originally when the lists were compiled by that judicial board which hon. gentlemen opposite think was so perfectly fair and just, in a great many cases the post office address was left out, but the section, township and range were given in almost every case and it was therefore quite easy to find the voters. The hon. member (Mr. Greenway) also said that qualified electors had to go hundreds of miles to get on the list and he said the member for Selkirk would endorse that statement. Well, my colleagues and myself have gone over the constituency of Selkirk and we have taken the last census map of the province of Alanitoba, and we have taken every polling subdivision in that constituency where a registration clerk is required by law to sit in the near future, and we have failed to find where a man would have to go fifty miles, much less one hundred miles to get on the list. Therefore I say that the member for Lisgar was wide of the mark when he said voters would have to go one hundred miles to get on the list. There is not a word of truth in it. He also found fault with the shortness of the time that elapses between the conclusion of the registration sitting and the court of revision ; but the province of Alanitoba is at the present time having new proclamations issued to extend the time so as to suit the fancy and meet the whims of hon. gentlemen opposite.
The hon. gentleman also said that the government of Alanitoba had deliberately torn froip the list of voters certain names. It has been said before, and I repeat it, that there was never such a thing done that was contrary to law. He also made the state-

ment that the Tories of Manitoba had undertaken to make some voters. Well, Sir, I want to say again that there is not a word of truth in that statement. The names that were put on the list were put on at the request of the Liberals of that particular polling subdivision. Now, who is this member for Lisgar? Is he the man?-yes, he is the man that went up and down this country for twelve years shouting: ' Hands off the province of Manitoba; equal justice to all, special privileges to none.' These were his war cries. Where is he to-day? He is the man who said to the government of the day: ' Give us our swamp lands, give us our school lands, give us our national schools.' 1 wonder where he is on that question today. He is the man who in those days stumped not only the province of Manitoba, but also the province of Ontario, trying to raise religious prejudices? Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we have all enjoyed the very amusing speech made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) this afternoon, but I do not believe it is worth taking up very much of the time of the House to follow him in any detail. He has travelled from confederation down to the present time and has tried to present the real or imaginary wrongs which he thinks Manitoba has suffered at the hands, not of this government, but at the hands of his own party. When he talks about lands, when he talks about mines, when he talks about the area and boundaries of the province of Manitoba and when he talks about the fish that float in the waters this government had nothing to do with these things, but the things of wrhich he complains were done when his owTn friends were in power. But there is one thing which the hon. gentleman has referred to which, in my mind, is very pertinent. He spent nearly half of his time, in fact, I think more than half, in trying to prove to this House and the country that an attempt was made by the government in 1903 to correct the wrongs, at least the alleged wrongs, which existed in the province of Manitoba at that time and which certain members on this side of the House contend exist at the present time. He has delved into the archives of some of the public departments at Ottawa and has produced an original document which he has placed upon the pages of ' Hansard ' and which he says is a Bill which was prepared for the purpose of providing for a special revision of the voters' lists in Manitoba in 1903. He tried to fasten this upon the knowledge of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who has denied that he knows anything about it, and I do not think that there is any hon. member of this House, or any person in Canada, no matter what his politics may be, but who will agree that the Prime Minister is telling the truth when he says that he has no
recollection of it. The important question is not whether the right hon. Prime Minister knew about this Bill, but the important fact is that in 1903 a condition of affairs existed that justified some person in attempting to pass legislation which would remedy that condition of affairs. To my mind that was the important question in 1903, and it is the important question in 1908. There has certainly been an agitation going on in the province of Manitoba for the last six years. That agitation has culminated in the introduction of the Bill which we are now discussing, and for a short time I wish to discuss the Bill as I view it, giving, to some extent, the reasons why I think it is necessary to introduce this Bill and the reasons why this Bill should become law. The arguments which have been addressed to this House by hon. members from the province of Manitoba, and I think nearly every hon. member from that province has taken part in this discussion, seem to show that there is existing to-day a state of affairs in regard to the voters' lists which does not exist in any other province in Canada, and which, if it did exist in the eastern portion of Canada, would lead almost to a riot. Imagine for a moment a man in the province of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Ontario being compelled to travel 00 miles to have his name put on the voters' list. Some hon. gentlemen from the province of Manitoba have stated that men are compelled to travel 100 miles to get their names on the voters' list. What would be said in the eastern provinces if people were subjected to an indignity and an iuconvenience of that kind ? As was stated by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) last evening, one of the great difficulties which people who take any interest in the preparation of the voters' lists have to contend with is the apathy of a great many voters in looking after the revision of the list and seeing that their nannes are placed upon it. If people in eastern Canada had to travel five miles to get their names put on the voters' list, in a good many cases there would be lots of names lacking from these lists. They would not go at all, as an hon. member says. But that is a matter that I will discuss a little later on. Before the present government came into power in the province of Manitoba there was an election law which our friends, then in opposition, now in control of the government, claimed to be unfair. I am not going to argue whether that law was fair or not. I am only mentioning it to show that there has been difficulty in the province of Manitoba for many years over the franchise. The cardinal features of that law, however, were that the government appointed registration clerks and that these registration clerks sat continuously at certain places in the province, or their offices were open continuously for four

weeks. During that time they would receive applications to add to or strike names from the lists. Then an interval of six weeks must elapse between that and the revision courts, and during that time these preliminary lists were posted in' public places in the constituency, in the post office, in the court house and in other public offices. Municipal officers, members of parliament and defeated candidates, both federal and provincial, received a copy of these lists and they had six weeks within which to file their protests and to have the lists cleaned up by revision. Our friends, then in opposition in the province of Manitoba, stated that when they came into power they would change that law and would pass a law which would work out more to the advantage of the people and which would be an improvement upon the law existing at that time. They came into power, I think, in 1890, and in the year 1902 they passed a franchise law which has been admitted by members on this side of the House to be fair, and which I must say appears to be fair. I am not going to give all the particulars of it, but the underlying principle of the law of 1902 was that a registration board, I think it was called, consisting of the county court judges, appointed the registration clerks and then they also assigned to themselves certain districts in which they sat as revising officers. But, Sir, here is where we commence to see the fine hand of the jiolitician in Manitoba, because, while the board had the right to appoint the registration clerks, the government, by order in council, took upon themselves the right to say when, where, for how long and under what conditions these registration clerks should sit. I am bound to say that in the year 1903 there seemed to be a goodly number of places at which people could apply to have their names added to the list. I am not going to weary the House by reading extracts. I have a list prepared by my hon. friend the member for Dauphin which gives the number of days, the number of places aud the registration clerks in each constituency in Manitoba from the year 1903 to 1908. Just here I want to point out a few inconsistencies and a few of the reasons why my hon. friends claim that the law was unfair. In the constituency of Arthur there were in 1903 nine places at which people could register their names before the clerks and in 1903 that number was reduced to one, and the registration clerk sat only on one day. The trouble, as I understand it, is not in the law of 1902, but in the administration of the law, and I think I might go as far as to say that there is not very much fault with the law of 1904. The fault is with the administration, tinder the Manitoba franchise law of 1902, which is said to be fair, and which would look to me to be fair from reading it, acts were done and things happened which would Mr. CARVELL
not be tolerated for a moment in eastern Canada. Again, at a place called Lac du Bonnet, which was a small district some thirty or forty miles from the registration place, the people could not leave their homes to come to the court, and the revising officer stated that if these people could not come to him he would be fair and go to them, and he went to them but he arrived on a date after the date fixed in the proclamation. He accepted the application of these men and placed thirty-eight of tjhem on the list, and no one denies that every man of them was entitled to be a duly qualified elector under the law of Manitoba. But when the election came in 1903 these thirty-eight men were denied the franchise simply because the revising officer had tried to carry out what ought to be the spirit of the law. There has been an attempt made by gentlemen opposite to show that the county court judge gave a different certificate for this registration from that which he gave in other cases, but that only shows the iniquity of the law which would prevent these men going on the list simply because the judge happened to make a different kind of certificate from the usual certificate. The fault is in the law; it is in the people who are adminstering the law in Manitoba, and the whole process by'which names are kept off the list or put on the list in that province is in need of being remedied. It is such things as that we complain about, and that is the reason why this legislation is introduced. Another instance, right in the city of Winnipeg a revising officer named Bonner closed his court while hundreds of people were waiting to be registered, and so great was the outcry raised by the Liberals and by the press and by fair-minded men generally, that the matter was taken to the courts on a writ of mandamus to compel this officer to open his court and give the people a chance to register, and in the Supreme Court of Manitoba in Regina verses Bonner (Volume 14. page 407) it was held unanimously by that court that the revising officer should* have continued his court open and that he had the same right as a county court judge had to adjourn the sitting from day to day until the sitting was finished. On that branch of the case the court of appeal held that this mau was wrong.
And the law right.

Yes, and I will say just now that because the law was right, at the next session of the Manitoba legislature the government took precious good pains to fix the law so that it would not be right again. Such was the agitation in Manitoba about this affair that this Bonner even applied for an order of contempt of .court in regard to what the newspapers were saying about him and the judges rightly held he was not entitled to any such protection. The case was dismissed without costs. In
all these matters, while the court had to held that Bonner was wrong, they gave no costs to anybody. But the contemptible part of it, one of the things that makes it necessary for this parliament to intervene, was the* fact that this man was allowed, with the connivance of the authorities of the government of Manitoba, between the time the application was made for the mandamus and the time fixed for the hearing, to return his papers, and thus give up all power to hold any revision; and consequently there was nothing to be gained by the court ordering the mandamus to issue. That is only a sample of the way the Conservative party manipulated things in Manitoba.
Will tlie hon. gentleman kindly say to the House who appointed Mr. Bonner revising officer?

As I understand, by the law of 1902 it was the county court judges. I am admitting that that law appears on its face to be fair ; but by the orders in council which the Manitoba government passed, when it came to be worked out, it was most unfair. These are a few of the things that happened in 1903. The agitation in the province became so great that the legislature at the next session had to try to pass legislation to meet some of these cases. I am going to show what they did. They practically repealed the law providing for the registration of voters. All the sections, I think, from 22 to 99 were repealed, and new sections enacted in lieu thereof ; and while I am not going to say that this is absolutely a new law, I am going to say that it is new in principle. Very many new principles were introduced into the Act which made it even worse than it was before. The cardinal change was in regard to the appointment of registration clerks. Trior to this amendment the registration clerks were appointed by the county court judges ; but by the legislation of 1904 that power was taken away from the county court judges and was placed in the hands of the Governor in Council, so that the registration clerks in Manitoba to-day are the appointees, the loyal supporters, in many cases the active workers, of the Manitoba government. The government also took to themselves the right to say when and where registration clerks were to sit, how many there should be in a constituency, how long they should sit and the dates and times they should sit. And remember, these registration clerks were not in the position of county court judges, and therefore, when the government prescribed that they should sit at certain places till five o'clock, when five o'clock came their jurisdiction was gone. I want to be fair to the hon. member for Marquette, who first brought up this matter. When he was delivering his speech, and I must say that it was an able speech from his standpoint, he pointed with a good

deal of pride to the fact that by a certain section of this law the registration clerks could sit after the clock struck the hour in certain cases ; and I submit that the hon. gentleman tried to leave the Impression on the House that notwithstanding that the time had been fixed by the order in council for the closing of the registration office, yet the registration clerk had the right to go on and finish up the business. If that was the intention of the hon. gentleman it was most unfair. That was the impression made on my mind, and I am satisfied that it was the impression made on the mind of the Prime Minister, because immediately afterwards he referred to it; but when you come to analyze the clause of the Act with regard to that, you find that it was only the persons present at the time the clock struck the hour for closing the registration office who had a right to have their grievances heard. The section with regard to that is section 26, subsection a, Which I will read, so that there may be no misunderstanding about it :
The registration clerk shall receive all applications of electors for registration, the striking off names of electors from the list, and for the correction of names on the list, who are present for that purpose at the time fixed for the conclusion of the registration sittings, notwithstanding that such applications are, in point of fact, received by the registration clerk after the hour of closing the registration sittings aforesaid.
My hon. friend said : here is the evidence that no man is going to be shut out from having his name put on the list. But my hon. friend took good care, when quoting the law of the province of Manitoba, not to quote section 48, subsection d, and I am going to read it for the benefit of my hon. friend. It says :
The following persons shall be entitled to bo present at sittings of the registration clerks for the purposes of this Act: ,
(d) Any person desirous of being present as a spectator; provided that no more than twelve persons, other than the persons before mentioned and officers in attendance, shall be entitled to be present at the same time.
When the legislature of Manitoba found that injustice had been done and that public sentiment had been created to such an extent that they had to do something to amend this law, pretending to be fair they provided that the registration clerk should have jurisdiction to go on and take the applications of all present at the time of the closing of the court, but they put in that rider that there could be only twelve persons in the room at that time. I ask hon. gentlemen again, if they call this British fair play.
They need not necessarily stop at five o'clock. Twelve could go on after five o'clock.

Twelve could go on, but suppose there were one hundred 7 Mr. CARVELL.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, That has not occurred.

It occurred in Winnipeg, and it occurred all over the country. I will come down to 1905 and show what occurred. I am going to refer to the press reports that appeared in Manitoba at the time these things happened, and I presume that there must have beeu foundation for these reports or they would not have been published. Here is the heading of a Winnipeg paper, I presume the ' Free Press,' of June 2, 1905 :
Hundreds of electors deprived of their votes. The one-day, one-place registration worked out as expected-citizens had to stand in line for hours to register. In South Winnipeg the law was ignored in interests of fair play. Hundreds unable to get access to booths- lively scenes-indignation at St. Boniface-registration elsewhere.
Then it goes on to give other particulars under these headlines. It was estimated that hundreds of people were prevented having their names put on the lists simply because the time limit fixed by that government was not sufficient for the work to be done. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite try to make the country believe that no one was deprived of the right of having his name registered on the list. A resolution was read here the other day, which I need not read again, from the labour council, in which the labour council claimed that hundreds of people were unfairly dealt with and were prevented having their names put on the list, and that council asked in strong terms for an amendment to the law. That was in 1905, and it shows how unjustly this law has worked out by order in council. In 1903-1904 there was a fairly good chance to put names on the lists, but in 1905 there was only one registration place in every county in Manitoba. Think of it-and that for only one day or a portion of one day.
Does the hon. gentleman say that there should have been just as many days for registration in 1905 as there was in 1903 7
Most certainly. The very iniquity of the law is now being voiced by the hon. gentleman.

I do not suppose I am allowed to explain why there should not be, but I ask the question whether there was the same need for as many days of registration in 1905 as there was in 1903. Everybody knows there was not.

I am surprised that my' hon. friend has the nerve to ask that question. What is the difference between an election list in 1903 and one in 1904 or 1905 7 Does my hon. friend not know that there is liable to be a by-election any day, that a man is liable to die and the consti-

tuency lie represents liable to become vacant ? That interruption only shows the perverted minds of the Tories of Manitoba. I want to tell my hon. friend how we do these things in the east. We have there a revision every year-an honest, full and complete revision. 1 would like my hon. friend to come down there and say to the municipal authorities in any district: Oh, there is not going to be an election this year, and therefore there is no reason to revise the lists.
That is not my reason at all.
That is the only inference any reasonable man can draw from my hon. friend's utterance. Because there was not an election in 1905, he says there was no necessity for a complete revision.
That is not my reason. Give me one minute only and I will explain.
You may ask any question you have a mind to.
Never mind him.

It only shows what a perverted idea the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has regarding the preparation of the voters' lists. His idea is that the voters' lists exist by and for the Tory party only, and should be prepared only when the Tory party wants to use them, and the ordinary elector or the ordinary man who happens to be a candidate has no right whatever. And it is because of this perverted idea that this parliament is asked to interfere and remedy this condition and so arrange that every man will have a fair show to be put on the lists. There is another reason which I may give and which my hon. friend need not accept, but it is the reason why this unfair advantage was taken, why there was only a chance given on one day at one place in a whole county for the putting on or striking names off the lists. And that reason was that the election of every Liberal except one was protested, and if those election trials went on, in all probability they would be settled in 1905, and by-elections would have to be held, and the Tory party did not want any chance given to have names put on the voters' list.
Were not also the elections of six Conservative members protested, and how therefore could there be any discrimination ?

The whole object of the Manitoba Act was discrimination. Its whole object was to give the Conservatives an unfair advantage over the Liberals. This seems to be what my hon. friends opposite have at heart.
You have not been posted right.
I will take the responsibility of whatever I say, and you need not blame it on my friends in Manitoba.
They had to stuff the lists if they wanted to keep in office.

There is another thing which my hon. friend from Souris dilated on yesterday, and he thought he had found a panacea which could be applied to any disease in the electoral body of Manitoba. When the right hon. the First Minister was speaking, my hon. friend could not contain himself and he asked the right hon. gentleman to read section 61. My right hon'. friend did read section 61, and it would have been well for the hon. member for Souris if he had, taken some advice from his legal friends before making that request. He had in his mind that this section 61 gives the county court judges power to enlarge the time in which to do any act regarding the preparation of the lists or the carrying on of elections in Manitoba. That evidently was his idea because that is the substance of what he said. Well, sections 22 to 51 inclusive deal with the registration clerks alone. Then from section 51 down to section 70, they deal with the revising officers, and let me point out that the revising officers are not necessarily county court judges. By a proclamation issued every year in the month of May, the government of Manitoba creates the county court judges a court of revision, but this court of revision has the power to appoint barristers of not less than three years standing to act in the place of the judges and carry on the business of registration, and they are called registration officers, and while they are sitting as such, they have the same powers as county court judges. But my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) will not claim that a man sitting as a revising officer is a member of the board of registration. I do not think the hon. member for Souris will claim that a revising barrister is a member of the board of registration, and it is only the board of registration which has the power to extend the time. Let us get down to a concrete example. The revising officer is holding his court, and according to the order in council that court ceases to exist at six o'clock. When six o'clock comes, has he the power, under section 61, to extend the time ? Not by any means. Has he the power to extend anything? No. Let me tell you what section 61 means. It means that after the Governor in Council have provided that a court will sit, say in Souris, for one day, from one to six in the afternoon, if the Board of Revisers think that time is not sufficient, they will have, before the revision takes place, the right to ex-

tend the time. If they think that sufficient time is not given between the close of the registration clerks' court and its opening, then they have the right to extend the time for their sittings. And I assert again that they have no power whatever over the registration clerks, they have no power whatever sitting as independent judges or revising officers to extend the time.
I never said they had.
But my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) implied that. He read this
I said the revising officers.
I wish my hon. friend would possess his soul in patience until I am through, and then he ^vill have his opportunity-
He admits that you are right.
Of course, he admits that I am right. And he knows that the only logical effect of his arguments and his quotations was that something else-
I rise to a point of order. I never admitted that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) was right, and I never said that this applied to the registration clerks.

The point is not well taken, Mr. Speaker, for the hon. gentleman admits that this is the only logical conclusion of what he did say.
Now, I think I have pretty well exploded the hon. gentleman's theory concerning section 61. Let us see now some further effects of this law of 1904. When the hon. member for Marquette was speaking, to show that there was no injustice in thisj case, that the law had been devised to meet every emergncy and

If the hon. gentle- | man (Mr. Carvell) would allow me, before he leaves the point with which he was dealing, I would like to refer him to the speech of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurler) on this point wherein he speaks of section 42. First the right hon. gentleman quoted the section as follows:
In case, by reason of interruptions or other emergency a sitting of the registration clerk is not commenced on the proper day, or is interrupted after being commenced and before the closing thereof, the registration clerk shall resume the, registration on the following day and so on from day to day within the hours hereinbefore limited, until the registration sittings have been opened and kept open without interruption, and with free access to persons desiring to be registered, for the full number of days provided in the proclamation to be issued under the provisions of this Act. The times limited for the registration of elec-Mr. CARVFLL.
tors shall be directory only, and any mistake or miscarriage in respect thereto shall not invalidate the list of electors of any electoral division.
After quoting this, the right hon. gentleman proceeded :
This seems to be perfectly fair, I have nothing to say against it. On the contrary I would altogether commend it. It provides that if the registration clerk, within the time allotted to him by the proclamation of the lieutenant governor, has not sufficient time to hear all the applications or to erase names or to do all the work he is commanded to do, he can extend the time.

The quotation of my hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) only shows the danger of laymen undertaking to interpret law. My hon. friend knows the English language well enough to know that that only provides that, in case something has happened by which the five hours, or whatever it may be, allotted by the Governor in Council has been interrupted, and the clerk has not been able to sit, he may sit the next day for the number of hours provided. The Prime Minister admitted that that was fair, and it is fair, as far as it goes. But my hon. friend knows- or, if he does not know, let him ask his leader (Mr. R. L. Borden) or any of the legal gentlemen on that side of the House -that I am right in my construction of the section and that it only means that if an interruption happens it is not to prevent the people having the five or six-or sometimes only two-hours granted by the munificence of this order in council, and that they may not be cheated of any portion of it. That is all it means. But the registration clerk cannot and will not extend the hour, and the hon. gentleman cannot find the section in the Manitoba law which says that the clerk can extend the time, or which allows him to do anything after the clock strikes except to take the applications of the twelve men who may be present at the booth to add their names to the list.
Now, I was going on, when my hon. friend from Marquette interrupted me, to refer to another provision which he referred to with great pride. He could not find the citation at first, though he said he knew that the provision was in the law; but his friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) looked it up and handed it to him. He quoted it in order to show the fairness of the law with regard to revising courts. The provision referred to will be found in section 65. subsection 11, and my hon. friend from Marquette read it with a great deal of pride and thought it settled the whole question. I think I can show him it does not settle as much as he thinks it does. It says :
The revising officer shall also receive and deal with the applications of all persons to be registered as electors who shall be present at

the time fixed for the closing of the court of revision, notwithstanding that the hour so fixed shall have elapsed.
Now, Sir, that provision gives the revising officer the right to hear the applications of men who are present at the time the clock strikes. What for? To have their names added to the list, but not to strike names from the list. And, as if this were not explicit enough, in the same section, by subsection 9, this government of Manitoba has provided that :
No complaints or appeals shall he heard by a revising officer to strike names off the list of electors, unless -applications therefor have) been \filed with the registration clerk asl hereinbefore by this Act provided.^
I stated a little while ago to an hon. gentleman on this side that I would show that the legislature of Manitoba, by their Act of 1904, not only did not extend the privileges granted under the previous law, but actually curtailed them, that if it corrected vices which existed in 1903, it actually made it harder for people to get a fair revision than it had been before. Now, the corn-paint from Manitoba members on this side of the House, as I understand it, is not so much of the impossibility of having names added to the list as of the impossibility of cleaning up the list: and my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), I think, gave the best illustration that has been given in this House of the unfairness of this feature of the law. I have not the citation here, but I can come within a hundred of his figures, and that is near enough when you talk of taking names off the list by the thousand. The hon. gentleman, in attempting to show the unfairness of the Greenway law, said that in the revision early in 18S9 or 1900, if I remember well, something like 2,500 names were struck off the list in the city of Winnipeg alone.
I rise to a question of privilege. The time to which I referred was before this government came into power at all.

I will take the hon. gentleman's word for that. But he said that they had succeeded in striking off 2,500 names, and this he cited as evidence of the injustice of the Greenway Act. Then came a remarkable admission. He went on to say that, in 1903, there were ten or fifteen names struck off; the next year ten or fifteen names struck off. And for this whole time up to the present he was only able to show that less than a hundred had been taken off the list. What greater condemnation do you want of this law and the manner of its administration than this statement of the hon. member for Souris? The whole burden of the cry of the representatives of Manitoba is that they cannot get names struck off the list. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) stated that in his division the only way they could get the list cleaned up was by agreement between the parties. So, let us see where we stand: You have a registration clerk, sitting we will say in the centre of a constituency which may be forty miles square-as distances run out there I think they would easily be as large as that. I am asking my hon. friends from the east to consider that situation of affairs. You have a man sitting there, we will say, in the centre of a district forty miles square. He says, I will sit here for two, or three, or four or five hours, if you will; come now with your applications. Consider that under those circumstances the whole county is being compelled to come to that one point. He says: Come on now with your applications to have the names struck off the list. You have a list of 400 or 500 names who do not belong there, and you have possibly two hours, in any case not more than five hours, to do all this work.
Would it take more than five minutes at the most to. file the applications.
But you have to take evidence, you have to see that these people have the right to come there. You have to take evidence in order to get the names on the list.
The hon. gentleman misunderstands me. I understand his complaint to be that you could not get the names off. Why, it would not take more than a minute or two to file a hundred applications.
It is not the question of time, it is the fact that a man has to travel 30 or 40 miles in order to get there.
Is there no party organization by which anybody on behalf of the party can put in a hundred names all at once ?
No, the merits of the case have got to be tried. I am speaking of adding on names, and every man going there himself, unless he is sick.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I thought he was speaking of the trouble of striking off names.

I am speaking of both. I am showing the unfairness of asking people to go 30 or 40 miles to get their names on. and I am also showing that unless they do go there and are present during those two hours, and unless they happen to be one of the 12 lucky men who are inside the registration booth at the time the clock strikes the hour, then they have no chance to file an application to remove names from the list. And if they do not get the chance, then I say that under this beautiful law which the hon. gentleman wants to perpetuate, the revising officer has no jurisdiction

to receive applications afterwards in his court to strike a name off the list in Manitoba to-day, so I am informed. It has been stated here by bon. members, and is not denied by the opposition, that there are thousands of names on the lists which have no right to be there.
Now 1 will not dwell any longer upon this specific instance of unfairness in the law, excepting to show what has taken place at the revision which is going on at tlie present time. Now there was an investigation before a committee of this House, I think in 1906, where evidence was given by both parties as to the condition of affairs in Manitoba at that time. It was known by the Conservative party in Manitoba two months ago that this Bill was going to be introduced and brought up for discussion. Now they are wily politicians, and the moment they found that their acts were going to be brought under the limelight and criticised by the people of Canada, the moment they found that remedial legislation was going to be enacted, then they become virtuous, and then hon. gentlemen opposite from that province stand up and say, see how virtuous we are to-day, look what we are doing to-day, why, we are giving you 6, 10, 12, 14 registration districts in each constituency, we are giving you two days in most cases for revision courts when you had only one before; we are giving you everything you ought to have, and everytmng that a reasonable man could ask. Also their leading Tory paper comes out with a challenge that they will give $25 to any man who fails to get his name on the list and complies with all the provisions of the Manitoba law. Well, why did they not make that challenge five years ago? The trouble was that the poor fellow could get no chance to comply with provisions of the law.
We have made the challenge retroactive.

Well, I have not seen that part of the challenge, I have seen the challenge which says they will give $25 to any man who fails in this revision to get his name on the list. Now I want to show what they have done in the division represented by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford), in their management or mismanagement of this application. We find that it is an Impossibility to appeal against names added or proposed to be struck off, in at least I think two districts in his constituency. We have shown that by the law there must be at least five days eiapse between the close of the registration court and the opening of the revision court. I think there must be one or two days for handing in the lists to the revising officer, and the revising officer must give at least three days notice to a person against whose name there is an appeal. Their orders in council show that there are only three days Mr. CARVELL.
between the last day for the sitting of the registration court and the revision court. Now I ask how is it possible to appea 1 against a name added, or to appeal against striking a name off the list, under those circumstances. Oh, they say, that is a mistake, and that is the reason why this law should be erased from the statute-book. Well, Sir, I say that if you have a law in Manitoba by which it is possible for a mistake like that to be made then you have abundant evidence that it is right and just for this parliament to intervene in order to cure the evil, so far as we are concerned, and to provide a law that will be fair, just and equitable to all parties concerned.
Now I want to discuss the thin red line matter, because if I do not they will say that we are afraid of that. There has been a good deal of discussion in the province of Manitoba and in the newspaper press of Canada over this thin red line. 1 think probably outside of Manitoba there has been more discussion over the red line than there has been over the unfairness and iniquity of the law itself. We find that When the returning officers received the lists in 1904 for the Dominion elections, in a number of cases there was an overlapping of constituencies, that is to say, a portion of a local constituency would be included in a federal constituency. In the constituency of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, we are told there are parts of seven local constituencies included, and there is not any entire local constituency Included in the federal constituency. That is true to some extent in all the constituencies in Manitoba. My hon. friends opposite now do not deny the right of the returning officer to arrange these lists so that the proper persons may vote in their proper places. They admit that now, because they are compelled to admit it. The other evening the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said .that in the prosecutions which followed the elections of 1904, there was no fraud, and no protest against fraud. You will find his remarks on page 8585 of 1 Hansard,' but I will not trouble the House with reading them. He stated that there were no informations against returning officers for correcting overlapping lists, but for internal redistribution, I think I am giving the substance of his statement.
Now, Sir, I am sorry that neither my hon. friend from North Toronto nor any other member of this House has placed upon ' Hansard ' the exact informations which were laid against these people. I admit that we people who are not on the ground are all discussing this question somewhat in the dark as far as that question is concerned, but I simply want to ask this question and I shall be glad if some hon. gentleman will answer it : If the informations were laid solely on account of fraud in redistributing internal constituencies why were these informations dropped ? If these

returning officers committed a fraud Upon the public I do not think there Is enough magnanimity and brotherly love in the Conservative party in Manitoba to drop such a beautiful chance of wreaking vengeance upon their opponents. If there was anything in these charges, if the thing was not a farce, why did they not go on with the prosecutions'? They have the sheriffs in their control, they have the juries in their control, they have all the machinery of the province of Manitoba, why did they not go on with the informations ? The only reason that has been given so far is that which has been given by the hon. member for Marquette who says :	Oh, well, politics
will creep in and you cannot get convictions. Of all the flimsy excuses I ever heard for dropping charges as iniquitous as this and charges involving such serious consequences this is certainly the flimsiest.
I never heard such a flimsy excuse in my life put forward by a great political party to explain the action that it took upon that occasion. Any man from the east is forced to the conclusion that it was done for political effect. He is forced to the conclusion that these officers were arrested on election day in order to influence the election on that particular occasion and that when these arrests did not influence the election and did not defeat the Liberal candidates, the object for which they were brought about was gone. No offence against the law had been committed and all these gentlemen could do was to drag the cases on for two years from court to court until finally they were brought up against a stone wall and when Mr. Leach demanded that there should be a prosecution the atorney general of the province of Manitoba took the only course open to him, went to court and publicly entered a nolle prosequi in all cases.
And then they distributed a few thousand dollars among their legal friends in Winnipeg.
That was only an incident.
That was all right, was it not ?

They have a right to do that and if ever hon. gentlemen opposite are in power they will distribute a few thousand dollars among their legal friends as well. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was eloquent last night over the omissions from this iniquitous Act. He said that it was an outrage upon the rights of the people to allow constituencies to remain vacant beyond a reasonable time after the vacancies occurred. I know that because they did wrong it is no justification for doing wrong now, and I do not think that there has been wrong done, but I simply want to point to the inconsistency of this hon. gentleman. If there is an hon.
gentleman in this House who is capable of being absolutely inconsistent it is the hon. member for North Toronto and the more inconsistent he is the more I admire the nerve of that hon. gentleman. That hon. gentleman can stand up and put forth a proposition which would cause any other man to be laughed down, hut because of his record of inconsistency and because we know what he will do, he is allowed to go on and make these statements without protest. Did he, when he was a member of the Conservative government, ever protest against allowing a constituency to remain vacant for more than a fortnight ?
Answer that.

Did he ever allow a government official to go around the country for the benefit of the Conservative party and take part in elections ? Does he remember that when he was running an election in the province of New Brunswick in 1896 that they would send for another thousand shingles, shingles meaning passes on the Intercolonial Railway, in order to bring Tory votes to the polls ? Does he remember that ?
No.

The hon. gentleman has a most convenient memory. I do admire his nerve every time he speaks. The first time I heard the hon. gentleman speak was when I was not more than ten years of age. I heard him addressing a temperance meeting and I thought it was the most magnificent speech that had ever been delivered up to that time.
Did it have any effect on you ?	,

It made nne believe at that time there was only one great man in the world and that was George E. Foster. But I have been completely undeceived on many occasions since then. I have been deceived by this hon. gentleman's inconsistencies and when I hear this hon. gentleman standing up and finding fault with the Liberal party because they have allowed constituencies to remain open six months, when I hear him condemning them for allowing their officials to take part in elections and when I hear him charging this government with trying to bribe the constituencies with public works I am forced to exclaim : O, consistency, thou art a jewel. I say it is another evidence of the impossibility of the Liberals in the Manitoba legislature getting justice from the Conservative majority. going to the legislature of Manitoba to" have any grievance redressed.

If the hon. gentleman is right, why do they not bring down the original, and let the Liberals see it. I notice that when I get on to some thing pretty vicious, my hon. friend always gets on his feet. Now, I have only this further to say, that I have no hesitation in voting for this Bill as it stands, though it does not go as far as I would like to see it go. I want to ask my hon. friends from the east what they would think of asking that a farmer's son who has just come of age should be compelled to travel even five miles to a registration court to get his name put on the list ? He would not do it. Compare this cumbersome system which the Conservative government of Manitoba have worked off on that province, *with the simple system that prevails in any of the provinces of eastern Canada. For instance, in the province of New Brunswick, the two county councillors for a parish, which means the same thing as a township in other provinces, and one member appointed by the government meet on or before the 10th of September, and they take any means of information they have-the voters' list of the year before^ the oath of any one who comes before them, or their own knowledge-and they make up a preliminary voters' list, and post that for something like six weeks in three of the most conspicuous places in the locality. Then they give notice that between the 20th and the 25th of October they will meet at a certain place to complete the list. They meet, and if anyone wants to have a name struck off or put on, he gives notice to that effect. But this is never done; I do not believe there have

been ten notices of this kind in ten years. On the general principle of the Bill, the instances of unfairness which I have given are enough to convince me at least, they have convinced the government, and I believe they have convinced the opposition, of the necessity of a fair revision ani some change in the present law. If they take the responsibility of holding up Supplies and bringing upon this country all the consequences that that course will entail, that is for them to decide ; but if they take that course, I do not think the Liberals of the Dominion of Canada will have very much cause to complain.

BORDEN (Carleton, Ont.) Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to follow the hon. gentleman into the many details which have occupied his attention while he has been endeavouring this afternoon to instruct the people of Manitoba as to the proper way in which to prepare their voters' lists. It is apparent that the hon. gentleman has come to the conclusion, very much to his own satisfaction at least, that the people of that province and their representatives in the legislature are not capable of framing laws under which the voters' lists shall be prepared for the provincial elections. The hon. gentleman seems to forget that under the policy deliberately adopted in 1885, by the party of which he is a member, and put into

practice by that party in 1898, to the people of each province in Canada has been delegated the power to deal with the franchise, not only so far as provincial elections are concerned, but so far also as federal elections are concerned. He seems to forget also that not only by the terms of his leader's speeches in 1885 and 1898, but also by the exact terms of the resolution moved by his leader in 1885, to the provinces of Canada was to be confided the duty, and has been confided the duty, of preparing the voters' lists upon which members of this House are selected. Having regard to these facts, he sees fit this afternoon, in a speech full of sound and fury, if nothing else, to inform the people of Manitoba of the ignorance and ineptitude of their legislator's, and to instruct them how the lists of that province should in his opinion be prepared. May I suggest to the members of this House that the speech which has just been delivered, shows the absolute absurdity of the government's proposal from the very first; because here we have 215 or 216 men, or as many of them as chose to be present for the purpose of hearing the hon. gentleman, listening to a long and somewhat rambling discussion which if proper at all, would have been proper in the legislature of Manitoba and not in the parliament of Canada. Is it to be pretended, under the principles which have been laid down by the Prime Minister of Canada, both since his advent to power and while in opposition, that the parliament of Canada is the proper tribunal to settle the franchise and to prepare the voters' list for the province of Manitoba ? Why, every word, every motion, uttered or proposed by the right hon. gentleman, both in opposition and since his advent to power gives an absolute denial to the whole trend of the argument of the hon. member for Carleton.
The hon. gentleman dilated upon events that have occurred in Manitoba, by which, as he asserts, some persons who were entitled to be upon the list are not found there, and some persons whose names should be omitted from the list appear there. Let me point out to him and every hon. gentleman in this House that under any system, whether it is a system of registration or based upon municipal assessment, injustices of that kind are bound to occur. Let me point out that frauds are bound to occur under any possible system. Why, the hon. gentleman, in his discussion of the preparation of the voters' lists in the province of New Brunswick, did not see fit to mention-undoubtedly for reasons very satisfactory to himself-the stuffing of the Rothesay ballot lists to the extent of 400 names. I have a complete history of that most outrageous swindle under my hand.
I shall not trouble the House with it today, but I venture to think that before

the discussion is concluded we shall have occasion to refer to it more in detail. It is sufficient to say that a list which should have contained* only ninety names, was found, when forwarded to the proper officers, to have had 400 names added to it; and from that day to this, although the matter was brought up in the legislature of New Brunswick and the government urged to take action by Mr. Hazen, the leader of the opposition and his supporters, no attempt whatever has been made to discover and prosecute the guilty parties and they have gone unpunished, to the infinite satisfaction no doubt of my hon. friend from Carleton.

Will the hon. gentleman not admit that the legislature took action the next session by striking those names from the list and providing by legislation against the possibility of such a thing happening again?
Yet the hon. gentleman complains against the Manitoba government for having done the same.
Because you did not remedy the wrong complained of.

The hon. gentleman says it was remedied at the next session of the legislature. I understood that proceedings were taken, in the first place, in the courts, and that those proceedings had resulted in striking the names off the lists. I am under the impression that application was made to the Supreme Court of New Brunswick to have the 400 names struck off which had been added by fraud to those lists. I am under the impression that a motion was presented in the legislature of New Brunswick calling upon the Attorney General of that province, now a member of this government (Mr. Pugsley), to take action by way of investigation and have the guilty men punished, but nothing was done.
My hon. friend is begging the question.
I am not.

I want to remind the leader of the opposition as well as my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) that the government of the day. of which the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) was then Attorney General, instructed counsel to appear on behalf of that local government in the case which was tried before the court, in order to uphold this stuffing of the lists.
The hon. gentleman is begging the question.

I thought the hon. gentleman was sensitive about frauds. He is apparently sensitive about alleged frauds in Manitoba, but absolute]- callous to
frauds in his own province. Let me read to him, for his information, the language of the Chief Justice of the province of New Brunswick with regard to that particular incident. The Chief Justice said of the crime;	.
For its enormity it is unparalleled in the history of this country and I should think that the law officers of the Crown, if there are any law officers of the Crown, ought to take some steps to bring the guilty parties to justice. These allegations are made, and it appears they are true, and I say then that some person has been guilty of forgery and perjury-some person has been guilty of an awful crime, the guilty persons are somewhere and ought to be punished. The proper list was given to Mr. Gilland and by some means it was altered and I think 400 names were added-it seems to me that it ought to be probed to the bottom and that the Crown officers ought to use what diligence is in their powrer to discover the offenders and if discovered they ought to be brought to justice.
Judge Landry said:-I think it is a very-brazen attempt to commit a most serious violation of the law, and includes forgery, perjury and theft.
At the session of the legislature immediately following Mr. Hazen moved :
That in the opinion of this House steps ought to be taken at once to discover, convict and punish the criminals.
Does my hon. friend from Carleton think that was a proper motion? Does he think it was one which should have commended itself to the government and legislature of New Brunswick?

Will my hon. friend be kind enough to answer me one question ? Will he not admit that at the next session of the legislature, the non-residents voters' lists were absolutely abolished and consequently this non-resident list was abolished, and there are no such lists in New Brunswick to-day except at St. John?

I do not dispute what the hon. gentleman says if he asserts it. I was not dealing with that particular phase of the subject. I was dealing with the failure of himself and his political friends in New Brunswick to take any steps whatever to discover the perpetrators of this crime and bring them to punishment. I invite an expression of the opinion of the hon. gentleman upon the merits of Mr. Hazen's motion, but I am bound to say that, with unusual modesty, he does not see fit to vouchsafe an opinion to the House. Let me point out what action was taken by his political friends in New Brunswick. The motion of Mr. Hazen was amended by a majority vote and the amendment declared that the House * expresses full confidence in the Attorney General and does not express any opinion as to what steps he should take.' Well, the Attorney General took no steps, and the



men who perpetrated the fraud have gone unpunished from that day to this. I want to illustrate that particular instance for the benefit of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. Before the right hon. gentleman entered this House a moment ago, I declared and I declare again, that the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) illustrates the absurdity of the position of the government in this matter. In that speech the hon. gentleman sought to convince 215 or 216 members of this House, gathered from all parts of Canada, that he knows best the proper method of making up the voters' lists for the province of Manitoba. We have the declaration of the right hon. gentleman himself, we have his motion in 1885 declaring that the people of the province of Manitoba are the proper judges of that, yet we have a long speech from the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in which he seeks to instruct the people of Manitoba how they should make up their voters' lists. Apparently he knows far better than they how to meet these difficulties of time and place and method, and what steps are necessary, so far as the provincial voters' lists are concerned, to be taken by the provincial legislature. He wishes to convince this House that he knows more about these matters than the local legislature can possibly know. In saying that, I am not departing at all from the attitude we took in 1898, but I shall come to that a little later on. What I seek now to impress on the House is that when you once recognize and	assert this
principle, affirmed by the party now in power, that to the legislature of each province shall be confided the duty of preparing its own voters' lists as well as regulating its own franchise, it is utter folly for any man to go into the details of time and place and method and seek to convince the two hundred and sixteen members of this House that the forty or forty-five members from Manitoba are so absolutely ignorant of their local requirements that they should be instructed by us as to what is the best and most convenient method of dealing with this matter for that province.
Now, I will not follow my hon. friend into the details into which he wandered this afternoon. I want to come for a moment to some of the observations of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier). That right hon. gentleman referred to the question of granting Supply. My hon. friend from North Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Toronto (Mr. Foster) was Finance Minister in 1896, and he has refreshed his memory by reference to the record. Now, the right hon. gentleman seems to think that he has not been treated with absolute fairness in the quotations from his speeches of 1885 made by my hon. friend fiom Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) and .myself. I do not know of any word in the right hon. gentleman's speeches which qualifies the express declaration of his motion, in 1885. That motion was as follows:	.
In the opinion of this House it is preferable to continue the plan which has been adopted ever since confederation of utilizing for the elections to this House the provincial franchise and- voters' lists.
That is absolutely plain, distinct and unqualified. But if the day comes when a fraud is committed against this parliament, when legislation of a hostile character is brought forward in the legislature, then it will be always open to this parliament to resume its own powers and to enact a franchise law of its own.
If these words are regarded by the Prime Minister as important, they merit a moment's attention. tion of Manitoba is concerned, there is not the slightest foundation for saying that such a condition exists. Then, the right hon. gentleman, in the concluding part of the sentence which has just been quoted, says that ' It will always be open for this parliament to resume its own powers and to enact a franchise law of its own.' I do not understand that the right hon. gentleman intended by that-though he may have a contrary impression-that the parliament of Canada was to have a franchise law of its own for one particular province or two provinces and was to confide to the legislatures of all the other provinces power to regulate their own franchise and prepare their own voters' lists.
Now, let us look a moment at the situation in the legislature of Manitoba. I have pointed out that, when the fraud to which I have alluded was committed in the province of New Brunswick, the leader of the opposition in the legislature, then Mr. Hazen, brought up the matter at once and asked that proper action should be taken by the government to bring to punishment the men who had been guilty of the crime. Does the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell), does the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), suggest to the House that the Liberal members of the legislature of Mantioba are so absolutely devoid of intelligence, of courage, that they will not or dare not bring to the attention of the legislature of that province any defects which exist in the electoral law? Is that the meaning of the argument? Up to the present time, I have not heard any hon. gentleman state to the House any case in the legislature of Manitoba where any amendments (has been brought forward and that amendment has been refused. Of what use is the party system in the province of Manitoba if the Lioeral members of the legislature are not prepared to come forward and put upon record their opinions of this law so far as they regard it as defective and unjust and to ask that that injustice and those defects should be remedied? In the province of Nova Scotia, if my memory serves me correctly, we have, on more than one occasion, asked the government of the day, asked the legislature of the province, that the present appeal to the partisan sheriffs of the province should be done away with and that
an appeal may be allowed to the county court judges in that province. And I say that the Conservatives of Nova Scotia today would acclaim, would hail with delight, any proposal to put in force in the province of Nova Scotia a measure so absolutely fair and reasonable as that which has been discussed so much in this House and which is to-day the law of the province of Manitoba. I have been surprised that so little fault could be found with this legislation of Manitoba. We know that the laws enacted by this parliament, even after most careful revision of two branches of the legislature, are over and over again found defective. We know that the government comes down every year with amendments. And this law, enacted by the legislature of Manitoba, under a Conservative administration has been subject to so little criticism that I say here that I believe there is not in the Dominion of Canada a single province which can show legislation more satisfactory, more fair and more effective than that which we have been discussing.
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) refers to municipal lists, and he fixes his faith on municipal lists. Let me point out to him that there may be partisan officers who create lists under a municipal system.
