Payzant, president of the Bank of Nova Scotia, a very large property owner in Halifax and Dartmouth, found his name absent from the list when the elections came on. George S. Campbell, one of the most prominent merchants In Halifax, a!so found that he had no vote in that election. Those are the only names I remember, but many others came to me and were intensely indignant to find that, although their names had been on the voters' lists for many years before that election, they were disfranchised, and there was absolutely no remedy.
From the decision of the partisan and biased revisers there is no appeal except to that of equally biased and partisan sheriffs. With one or two exceptions these men are appointed to their positions merely upon the ground of some party service and their former occupations was not such as to qualify them to interpret such an Act.
I do not desire to be understood as reflecting upon all the sheriffs of Nova Scotia. On the contrary, I may mention Mr. Donald Archibald, sheriff of the county of Halifax. Although a strong Liberal, and a Liberal candidate on many occasions, and a member of the legislature, he is as fair a man as there is in the Dominion of Canada. I have perfect confidence in his justice and in his integrity in every way. Unfortunately there are sheriffs in the province of Nova Scotia of whom that can by no means be said. There are sheriffs in the province of Nova Scotia who are regarded and I believe justly regarded, as absolutely part of the Liberal organization, of the Liberal machine, for the particular county In which they are appointed.
The most of them refuse to give tbeir decision during the bolding of tbeir court for the reason that jthey would be then supposed to support their decision with argument. A notable case of this kind is sheriff Edwin Gates of Annapolis.
Arthur Carter of Deep Brook was last year assessed for over $500 but the revisers refused to register his name and an appeal was made to the sheriff. The assessment roll was pro-dued to the sheriff who admitted that the name should be registered, but when the final list was filed with the county clerk the name was not on. Robert Craig applied to be registered at Miidleton on income qualification. The revisers nut him on although the law [DOT] requires an income voter to register where he

resides and Craig did not reside in this district. This was admitted before the sheriff and the name was decided to be dropped but it, appeared on the final list.
I would like to mention in this connection that to such an extent has this evil gone in the county of Annapolis in particular, that men in that county, one man at least,, brought an action a few years ago against the revising officer for intentionally omitting his name from the 1st. and he got judgment for $200 and costs against the revising officer. Nevertheless he was disfranchised.
At Torbrook Mines in the same county fifteen miners made personal applications accompanied by affidavits showing qualification and were registered by the revisers. An appeal was made to the sheriff to have them struck off and in the absence of a tittle of proof the sheriff dropped these names.
At a trial of a reviser for failing to put into the sheriff original papers on an appeal, sheriff Gates admitted in September 1906, that he added the name of Millidge Best to the voters' list in polling district No. 1, notwithstanding that the name was ruled off by the advisers and no appeal was taken from the revisers' decision.
He gave as his excuse that he had received a letter from some one stating that Best was qualified.
That is the character of the judicial revision of the lists imposed upon the Conservatives of Nova Scotia. I would ask the right hon. gentleman in all fairness whether in view of all these illustrations he does not think that his attention should be centered to some extent upon Nova Scotia and that it should not be wholly devoted to the province of Manitoba where a Conservative governrnet happens to be in power.
Very frequently names are found on the final lists which were never before the revisers court or the sheriff on appeal. It is impossible to tell who does this padding, W'hether it is the sheriff or the clerk in whose custody the lists are placed. In either event there is no punishment provided for the culprit who does it.
I have already said, under any system there will be injustice even without any intent to defraud, or at least that which you might call injustice. Men will not make their applications in time or some default of that kind will occur. My hon. friend from Carleton spoke of men whose names were not upon the lists in Manitoba, but he did not tell us what diligence these men had used to get their names upon the lists. It is impossible to make any statute which will provide against the negligence of voters or the inaction of the party to which they may happen to belong. So long as you find a statute which is clear and plain and ordinary reasonable upon its face, it does not seem to me there is any justification for interfering simply because a particular political party happens to be in power at the time being in any province.
My right hon. friend was pretty frank about his motive for interfering in this case and I would direct the attention of the House to his argument at page 8572 unrevised ' Hansard ' where he said :
But, Sir, I ask my hon. friends if they will not admit that although the legislation which to-day exists in Manitoba and the manner in which it is administered may be satisfactory to the Tories it is not satisfactory to the Grits, and that is the reason why we have introduced this legislation.
Well, that is a pretty plain and frank statement on the part of the Prime Minister, but after ail what does it amount to? It amounts to this: The Liberal party moved a resolution in this House in 1885 that the principle of observance of the provincial voters' lists should be followed ; in 1898 they came into power and they put that principle into operation by placing the Dominion Franchise Act upon the statute-books. and then in 1908 they come to us not to make a new Franchise Act, not to revert to that policy which they condemned when in opposition and when in power as well, but to declare to this parliament that because under the legislation of Manitoba, under the administration of the government selected by the people of that province, the voters' lists are not satisfactory to the Liberal party, therefore this parliament of Canada shall legislate. To what result Will that lead us in this country? When the Conservative party comes into power, assuming that the present system of provincial lists is adhered to, what would be expected of them? Are they to adopt the same principle ? With respect to the province of Quebec or the province of Nova Scotia if the government of these provinces should be Liberal, are the Conservatives in power at Ottawa to come to this parliament and say :	We will leave British Columbia
alone, we will leave Ontario alone, we will leave Manitoba alone because our friends are in power there but we will go into Quebec and Nova Scotia and make voters' lists of our own in those provinces. Is that the principle which my right hon. friend proposes in all seriousness as a principle which should be carried out by either political party in this country ? It does not seem to me it would make for good government. So long as you adopt this principle of provincial voters' lists, who are the best judges in respect of time and place and convenience and method in any province. Can the 215 members of this House judge better for the province of Manitoba, or of British Columbia, than can the people of these provinces by their representatives in the legislatures. If they can, why is it that the 215 members of this House cannot judge better for the province of Quebec and the province of Nova Scotia than can their legislatures.

I once more confess that I am utterly unable to discover any real considerations of public policy which could justify the government in proceeding with the first clause of this Bill. You must deal with the franchise either on one principle or the other. It was open to the rigtht hon. gentleman in 1898, and it is open to him still to adopt a Dominion non-partisan franchise and to give the preparation and final revision of the voters' lists all over Canada to the judges and to persons appointed by the judges in order that there might be no suspicion of partisan interference. That would be a perfectly intelligible principle for the hon. gentleman to proceed upon ; it is one which I could understand and I think appreciate, or it was open to him to adopt the principle which the right hon. gentleman did adopt in 1898 by giving to each province in Canada the full right to determine the franchise and prepare the voters' lists not only for the election of members to the provincial legislature, but for the election of members to this House as well. There are the two systems, and the latter system has been adopted by the government. Then comes the question which has been raised by the right hon. gentleman as to what shall be our duty when any complaint is made from any province that the voters' lists are not fair. Well, Mr. Speaker, assuming that you do not depart from the right hon. gentleman's words reiterated over and over again in 1898, no matter what takes place this is a question for the people of each province. And in any case if you depart from that system, you could only depart from it in a reasonable way and by means of a reasonable inquiry. Therefore I say it would be absolutely unheard of discrimination, invidious, impolitic, unjustifiable to attempt to do this without the fullest possible investigation and inquiry by this House into the systems of every province in Canada. Why should the system of Manitoba be inquired into and their voters' lists superseded simply because the Liberal party is in a minority in the legislature there; why should you refrain from inquiring into the evils that I have brought to the attention of the House in the province of Nova Scotia? I do not doubt that if you examine the systems prevailing in the province of Ontario, or of Quebec, or of New Brunswick for that matter, you would find that just as serious errors and as many injustices have taken place under their systems as are alleged to have taken place "in the province of Manitoba. The principle is a vicious one which says that because the Liberal party is in power in certain other provinces but in a minority in Manitoba, therefore the power of this parliament shall be directed against Manitoba and not against Nova Scotia and Quebec.	'

There is no statesmanship in that, there is no good sense in that, there is nothing in it which will commend itself to the judgment of the people of this country. If the right hon. gentleman and his followers desired any investigation into the laws of the various provinces, or into the administration of those laws with respect to the preparation of voters' lists, why did they not bring down this Bill on the first day of this session, have that inquiry made and let us determine whether any unfairness or injustice prevails by reason of the laws of Manitoba, British Columbia, Quebec, Nova Scotia, Ontario or any other province which requires correction by the people of this country through their parliament ? Statements have been bandied about frbm the other side of the House and controverted on this side of the House, and you say that you shall lay hands on the province of British Columbia and the province of Manitoba simply because the Liberal representatives of these two provinces are complaining that they want different lists, that they want lists prepared by their own partisans. This Bill, when it was first brought down, was so absolutely absurd that I am astonished that the Prime Minister should have ever lent his name to its introduction. What was the proposition? The proposition was that because the voters' lists in Manitoba and British Columbia were prepared under the administration of persons appointed by the Conservative governments of those provinces, with recourse, in every case, to judges of the county court as the ultimate authority to decide upon the addition or subtraction of any name, therefore you put all that to one side as being partisan and unfair and you appoint your own partisans, without any express or effective reason that there should be the slightest appeal to any judicial authority. A proposition of that kind needs only to be stated to be laughed out of any House of Commons or out of any legislature in the country. If there is any good reason why these lists in Manitoba should be dealt with by this parliament, let us have an inquiry and an investigation and I am prepared to stay here to make it if the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House (are prepared to do so. It was the duty of the government to have had it made long ago. But let us not, in the language of the Prime Minister, seek to impose new lists upon the province of Manitoba simply for the reason that the right hon. gentleman's friends in Manitoba come to him and complain that these lists are not satisfactory. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but there iis another observation that I would like to make, .and it is one which deserves to be emphasized. You are proposing to do this in Manitoba and British Columbia without the slightest question as to the fairness of the lists having been raised in the legislature of either province. Are the Liberal

members of the legislature of Manitoba, or the Liberal members of the legislature of British Columbia so absolutely devoid of intelligence, common sense and courage that they do not bring to the attention of the Jegislature and the people of those provinces these alleged defects which have been proclaimed before this House. What is the [DOT]meaning of it ? If this government concluded that there was in the complaint of jts partisans in Manitoba-I have not heard any complaint by its partisans in the province of British Columbia-any ground for the amendment of the law, or for reform in the administration of the law, why did not this government, having once adopted the system of provincial voters' lists, make representations on that subject to the governments of British Columbia and Manitoba ? Has there been one word, one syllable, directed to either government, to the /government of British Columbia or to the government of Manitoba, pointing out these complaints, asking them for their reply before parliament should proceed to interfere .with the voters' lists of these provinces V One would have thought that that would have been the reasonable and proper course for the hon. gentleman to take before he sought to introduce this Bill.
With regard to the right hon. gentleman's proposals made in this House last night, I frankly confess that I am not fully able to understand perfectly just exactly what the Prime Minister did intend to suggest. I have no doubt that he will make me acquainted with his intentions; in fact he has promised to do so. But, at the present time I understand that the Prime Minister proposes that the allocation of voters in a polling division cut in two by the boundary of a federal division shall be made, not as it is now by the returning officer within any riding, but by a county court judge. There has been no difficulty, outside of Manitoba, in doing that. There would be no difficulty in Manitoba in doing that provided the returning officers discharged their duties honestly and impartially and with a full sense of their responsibility. But, inasmuch as we have had some experience in Manitoba pointing to the conclusion that this is not always the case, we are quite prepared to accept the hon. gentleman's proposition which we regard as a desirable one from that standpoint, so that there may be no suspicion by one party or the other as to the manner in which these voters are allocated.
But, beyond that whether the right hon. gentleman intends to adhere absolutely to the terms of this Bill or not, I do not know. I think he said that he was not wedded to its terms, but that is a very general expression indeed and I confess that I have not been able so to seize myself of the hon. gentleman's intentions in regard to the Bill as to understand that he is willing to make
any considerable departure from its terms. We think, on this side of the House, subject to what I have already said, that the first section of the Bill ought to be, withdrawn altogether. We do not consider it fair that twro provinces which have reasonable laws upon their statute-books for the preparation of the voters' lists, should be singled out merely for the reason that some persons w7ithin those provinces have made complaints to this government as to the alleged unfair operation of those laws. I do not think that you should propose to amend laws for such reasons or in that way.
We believe further, that you should certainly withdraw or completely modify the provisions of section 17. I am disposed to believe, from what the Prime Minister said in that regard, that it is not his desire or intention to interfere with the secrecy of the ballot. I firmly believe that he is impressed as much as I am with the necessity of preserving that as a vital principle of our election law. The right hon. gentleman has pointed out, and his Minister of Justice has also pointed out, that cases may occur where men are disfranchised through inadvertent marks or through marks made by design upon one ballot or upon a number of ballots. It has been pointed out that all the votes at a particular poll might be thrown out simply because a mark has been placed inadvertently upon the ballots. Even if there were no other remedy than that which the right hon. gentleman suggests.
I would not be disposed to concur in the provisions of section 17, because I would regard it as infinitely preferable that we should have a new election now and then, wherever that did occur, than that we should place on the statute-book of this country an amendment w'hich would have the effect of absolutely destroying the vital principle of our election law. I was rather surprised, on looking pretty carefully over the election Act some days ago for this purpose, to discover that among the sections providing for punishment there seems to be no particular section aimed at the returning officer who shall make any marks on the ballots before he p'aces them in the box. There is a general provision under which I think he would be included, but there is no special and distinct provision relating to that offence by a returning officer.* I would be inclined to suggest, instead of the proposed legislation, that the instructions to every deputy returning officer should be made so absolutely plain and distinct that he could not fail to understand their important meaning, and that a special provision should be placed upon the statute-book for the punishment of any deputy returning officer who should fail to comply with those instructions. I would not be inclined to limit the punishment to the man who did it intentionally ; I would hold that the man who did it even

by inadvertence and negligence should be subject to some measure of punishment, leaving it in every case to the discretion of the judge to dismiss him with a nominal fine or a reprimand. If you would put a provision of that kind on the statute-book, I think you would find it more in the interest of the country than that which is proposed by the government.
Lastly, I would invite the attention of the Prime Minister to the question of absolutely simultaneous elections in this country. We have this for the most part, but there are some cases of deferred elections in the pro-ince of British Columbia and in the province of Manitoba, and there may be one or two in the province of Quebec. I do not profess to speak for the province of Quebec on that point, but bow to the superior knowledge of my friends from that province. But I have made pretty careful inquiry with regard to all the provinces except the province of Quebec, and I am thoroughly satisfied that there is no need whatever of postponing any election except the election in the Yukon. I concede at once that that election would have to be postponed. In the province of British Columbia the provincial elections are held all on the same day. That was the case in the last provincial election, and I am assured from a great many sources in that province that there is absolutely no need whatever for postponement.
The Prime Minister has appealed to me in a portion of his speech for fair and reasonable consideration of this Bill. I may say to him in all sincerity that I have endeavoured to give it a fair and reasonable consideration, and I think that I have done so ; but I cannot bring myself to that condition of mind which would justify me in concurring in the imposition upon the province of Manitoba or upon the province of British Columbia of such an invidious and unjustifiable discrimination as that which I find to be contained in the first clause of this Bill.
Mr. GALLIHER moved the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to. and debate adjourned.

I wish to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister, as the ministers who have control of this service are not in their places, a paragraph in one of our papers which says that the Anglo-American cable from Prince Edward Island to the mainland was broken on Saturday. As the right hon. gentleman knows, this is a service w\hich is under the control of the Dominion government. This is an old cable which has been in use for thirty years, and we have often called the attention of the government to the necessity Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
of laying a second cable. The province is now without telegraphic communication, and I would like to know what the government propose to do in the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that we have any jurisdiction over a matter of this kind. If my hon. friend has any suggestion to offer, we would be glad to help him if we have the power.

The suggestion I made some time ago was that we should have a second cable. When the cable was broken over a year ago, I called the attention of the government to this necessity. Now it is broken again, and the whole province has to depend only on the steamers for communication with the mainland. I am merely calling the attention of the government to the matter, and I hope thev will act with despatch in regard to it.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.
